text_blocks.snippet: High blood pressure (hypertension) usually has no noticeable symptoms, which is why it is often called the "silent killer".

list.snippet: Asymptomatic: Most people with high blood pressure feel completely fine and do not experience warning signs for years.
Regular Monitoring: The only reliable way to know your status is to measure your blood pressure with a cuff.

General Guidelines: Normal blood pressure is below 120/80 mm Hg, while hypertension is consistently at or above 130/80 mm Hg. You can learn more about clinical definitions and background through the Mayo Clinic or the CDC.

text_blocks.snippet: Potential Signs of Extremely High Blood Pressure
When blood pressure spikes significantly or reaches severe levels, subtle or acute symptoms may occur: The National Council on Aging (NCOA)

list.snippet: Early-morning headaches: Persistent, dull pain at the back of the head upon waking.
Dizziness or light-headedness: A woozy feeling from reduced blood flow.
Vision changes: Blurred vision, double vision, or blood spots in the eyes from damaged retinal vessels.
Shortness of breath: Getting winded easily during light physical activity.
Heart pounding: Pounding sensations or rapid fluttering in the chest, neck, or ears.
Frequent nosebleeds: Unexplained or recurrent nosebleeds during sudden spikes.
Fatigue or confusion: Unusually low energy or trouble concentrating.

text_blocks.snippet: Blood pressure readings over 180/120 mm Hg require immediate emergency medical attention if accompanied by acute organ damage:
